5	visual-token budget lose the high-frequency detail needed to read small text or recognise small objects.
6	ViCrop is a training-free remedy: the MLLM's own attention or gradients locate the region relevant to the question,
7	that region is cropped from the original-resolution image and zoomed to the encoder resolution, and the crop is given
8	to the model *together with* the global image. We re-implemented the three ViCrop localisers (**rel-att**,
9	**grad-att**, **pure-grad**) and the adaptive box selection from scratch. We evaluated them on a seeded random
10	subset of TextVQA-val (no OCR tokens), using **LLaVA-1.5-7B** (n = 102) and **Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct** at a 448×448
11	pixel budget (n = 200). We also ran the demo-image experiment (Experiment 1) as fixed-option multiple-choice
12	questions. All of this ran on a shared CPU node.

30	The vision encoder sees a 336×336 (LLaVA-1.5) or ≈448×448 (our Qwen2.5-VL budget) rendering of the image. A

{"type": "content", "content": "I re-implemented the training-free cropping method (ViCrop) and tested it on LLaVA-1.5-7B and Qwen2.5-VL-3B. The report is at `report/report.md`, and all 22 figures it references are in `report/images/`. On a random subset of TextVQA (no OCR tokens), the two attention-based crop-selection methods (rel-att, grad-att) each improve accuracy by about 8–12 points, significantly on both models.

**Main results** (accuracy in %; points are the change from the no-crop baseline; p-values are paired tests):

| Model | Baseline | rel-att | grad-att | pure-grad | Random crop, same size |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| LLaVA-1.5-7B, n=102 (planned) | 49.6 | **61.9** (+12.3, p=0.004) | **61.2** (+11.6, p=0.007) | not run | 56.2 |
| LLaVA-1.5-7B, n=178 (extended) | 50.8 | 62.5 | 62.5 | not run | 53.9 |
| Qwen2.5-VL-3B, 448² budget, n=200 | 73.9 | **83.9** (+10.0, p<0.001) | **81.8** (+7.8, p=0.001) | 78.6 (+4.8, not significant) | 78.3 |

- **Where the crop goes matters, not just adding a zoomed view.** rel-att beats a random crop of the same size on Qwen (+5.6 points, p=0.004) and on the extended LLaVA set (+8.5 points, p=0.007). pure-grad puts its crop on the evidence about as often as a random crop does (42% vs 46%), and it scores the same as the random control.
- **The gain comes from small details.** On the half of questions with the smallest evidence, LLaVA goes from 44.6 to 70.6 and Qwen from 66.0 to 81.2. On large evidence there is almost no change.
- **The models do know where to look.** rel-att and grad-att crops contain the answer region in roughly 85–93% of questions. Raw attention in the same layers is nearly as good on TextVQA. Normalising by attention to a generic prompt (what rel-att adds) matters mainly when one image token soaks up attention regardless of the question. That happens with the multiple-choice prompts in the demo.

**Demo experiment.** The four multiple-choice questions and their options were fixed before any model ran.
- **LLaVA:**
  - The squatting person with the yellow backpack is "walking" at baseline and "squatting" with rel-att (p=0.99).
  - The backpack colour is fixed only by the version that tiles the large 2250×1500 image.
  - Asked open-ended, LLaVA misreads the date as "02/29/2012", and both rel-att and grad-att give the correct "02/20/2012". In multiple-choice form it picks option A for every input, including a crop placed by hand on the date. That is an answer-format failure, not a localisation one.
- **Qwen:** It already answers the demo1 questions correctly. Its maps miss the small person in demo2, and of the automatic methods only tiled grad-att fixes the backpack question. A crop placed by hand on the target fixes both demo2 questions for both models, so the resolution problem itself is real.

**Things to keep in mind:**
- **Subset sizes.** This ran on a shared CPU-only node with no GPU, so it covers 102–200 TextVQA questions, not the full 5,000. I stopped the LLaVA extension at 178 when compute ran out.
- **Answer-region boxes.** TextVQA has no answer boxes here, so I had Qwen draw them. They were used only to choose layers and for the localisation diagnostics, never to place an evaluated crop. Qwen's diagnostic numbers may be flattered because the boxes come from the same model.
- **Qwen resolution.** Qwen ran at a deliberately limited 448×448 pixel budget to mimic the low-resolution setting. I started a full-resolution Qwen baseline for comparison but had to stop it because the node was overloaded.
- **Demo size.** The demo is four questions and is illustrative only.

The code in `code/` reproduces everything in the order listed at the end of the report. I also saved two short memory notes covering this node's slow per-connection downloads (opening many connections in parallel gets around it) and these results."}
